title: Deployment types and capacity: PAYG, global, data zone, PTU
summary: Azure sells model capacity as pay-as-you-go Global, Data Zone or regional Standard, as Priority processing, and as provisioned throughput (PTU). The choice follows traffic shape, residency and how tightly latency must hold.
useIf: You must pick how to buy tokens for a production workload and defend the choice with numbers.
avoidIf: Traffic is unknown. Start on Global Standard, measure, then size commitments.

explain.md: Foundry offers `GlobalStandard`, `DataZoneStandard`, `Standard` (a single geography), the provisioned types `GlobalProvisionedManaged`, `DataZoneProvisionedManaged` and `ProvisionedManaged`, the batch types `GlobalBatch` and `DataZoneBatch`, and `DeveloperTier`. Microsoft advises starting with Global Standard. Global may process in any region, Data Zone stays inside the US, EU or APAC zone, and Standard stays in one geography; data at rest stays in the designated geography. Global and Data Zone Standard are not a failover: if the primary region has an interruption, all traffic initially routed to it is affected, so neither replaces a second region [[r5]].

**PTU** capacity is held whether or not requests arrive. It is billed per PTU per hour or through 1-month or 1-year reservations. Quota is per subscription, region and deployment type, and **quota does not guarantee capacity**; neither do reservations, so create the deployment first. Cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity [[r6]]. **Priority processing** is a pay-as-you-go tier set per deployment or with `service_tier: "priority"` per request. Its target is a p50 token rate per 5-minute window, not a per-request guarantee [[r10]]. **Spillover** sends non-200 overflow from a full PTU deployment to a standard one in the same resource, for all requests or per request through `x-ms-spillover-deployment` [[r7]].

explain.title: PTU sizing
explain.expr: normalized TPM = peak RPM x prompt tokens x (1 - cache rate) + output-to-input ratio x peak RPM x response tokens; PTUs = normalized TPM / input TPM per PTU, rounded up to the model increment

vars.v: model specific, from the sizing doc
smallest step of PTUs for that model

explain.example: Doc example: 1,000 RPM, 200-token prompt, 20-token response, ratio 8, 3,400 input TPM per PTU, increment 5. 360,000 / 3,400 = 105.88, so 110 PTUs. At a 50% cache rate it is 260,000 / 3,400 = 76.47, so 80 PTUs [[r7]].

whereToUse: Launch planning: Global Standard first, then measure peak RPM and token mix
EU-resident workloads: Data Zone Standard or Data Zone Provisioned
Business-hour apps with bursts: Priority processing instead of a commitment
Steady high-volume APIs with p95 targets: PTU plus spillover
Cost reviews: compare reservations with measured utilization

use: Provisioned: traffic is predictable and high enough to keep PTUs busy
Priority: latency matters but traffic is bursty
Data Zone: a residency boundary applies
Spillover: provisioned baseline with occasional peaks
avoid: PTUs for small or spiky traffic: capacity bills while idle
Assuming a quota or reservation gives capacity in a region
Spillover for Azure DeepSeek or Meta Llama, which are not supported
flips: A high prompt cache rate lowers PTU count, so redesign prefixes before sizing
A new residency rule moves you from Global to Data Zone and may delay model availability
Traffic becomes steady 24 hours a day: reservations beat hourly PTU billing at high utilization

pitfalls.symptom: A PTU deployment cannot be created despite a reservation
pitfalls.cause: Quota and reservations do not guarantee regional capacity
pitfalls.fix: Create the deployment first, then buy the reservation; keep a second region in mind

pitfalls.symptom: PTU bill is high and utilization low
pitfalls.cause: Sized for peak on spiky traffic
pitfalls.fix: Size PTUs for the baseline, spill the peaks over to Standard, and use Batch for async work

pitfalls.symptom: Cache breakpoints have no effect on a PTU-M deployment
pitfalls.cause: PTU-M keeps caching but has no breakpoints and no `cache_write_tokens`
pitfalls.fix: Order the prompt for implicit reuse; count cached tokens as free capacity

scenarios.title: Steady API inside an EU boundary
scenarios.situation: An internal API serves a steady 800 requests per minute around the clock. A p95 latency target exists. Policy keeps processing inside the EU.
unknowns: What is the prompt cache rate?
Is capacity available in the target region?
What does the model's increment of PTUs look like?
scenarios.question: How do you buy capacity?

options.name: Data Zone Provisioned sized for the baseline, spillover to Data Zone Standard
options.why: Steady volume keeps PTUs busy, the zone satisfies residency, and spillover covers peaks.
options.tradeoff: Idle cost if volume drops, and capacity must exist before you commit.

options.name: Global Standard
options.why: Global may process outside the EU, which breaks the boundary.
options.tradeoff: Right when residency is not a constraint and traffic is variable.

options.name: Priority processing in a Data Zone
options.why: No commitment and better latency than plain Standard.
options.tradeoff: Only a p50 target per 5 minutes, and a price premium at steady volume.

flips.if: Traffic falls to a few hundred requests a day
flips.then: Drop PTUs for Data Zone Standard.

flips.if: A prefix redesign lifts the cache rate to 50%
flips.then: Resize down: the sizing example falls from 110 to 80 PTUs.

scenarios.takeaway: Steady, residency-bound traffic favours provisioned capacity with spillover.

scenarios.title: A business-hours copilot
scenarios.situation: A copilot is used from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays with sharp morning and post-lunch bursts. Latency matters during bursts. The team wants no multi-month commitment.
unknowns: How strict is the latency target?
scenarios.question: Which mode fits?

options.name: Priority processing on a Global Standard deployment
options.why: It targets stable token rates during bursts without capacity held overnight.
options.tradeoff: Premium price, and the target is a p50 per 5 minutes, not a per-request guarantee.

options.name: Plain Global Standard
options.why: Cheapest, fine if bursts are mild.

options.name: PTU sized for the burst peak
options.why: Capacity is paid for at night and weekends and sits idle.
options.tradeoff: Right when traffic is high and steady all day.

flips.if: A hard latency SLA is contractual

flips.then: Re-run the PTU sizing and compare with reservations.

scenarios.takeaway: Bursty traffic is a Priority case. Provisioned capacity is for steady load.

scenarios.title: A pilot heading to production
scenarios.situation: A pilot has a few hundred users. Production is expected to be ten times larger, but nobody has measured token mix, cache rate or peak RPM.
unknowns: Can the pilot log RPM and token counts per request?
What is the lead time for PTU capacity in the target region?
scenarios.question: What is the plan?

options.name: Stay on Global Standard, instrument tokens and cache rate, size PTUs from measured peaks
options.why: The sizing formula needs peak RPM, prompt and response tokens and cache rate, all of which the pilot can measure.
options.tradeoff: Costs a pilot cycle before any commitment saving.

options.name: Buy a one-year reservation up front based on projected users
options.why: A reservation does not guarantee capacity and the sizing inputs are guesses.
options.tradeoff: Right once utilization is measured and stable.

options.name: Use Flex processing for production
options.why: Flex has no SLA and can return 429 for lack of capacity, so interactive users suffer.

flips.if: Measured utilization is steady above a PTU break-even
flips.then: Move the baseline to PTUs and spill over.

flips.if: Launch needs capacity guarantees in three weeks
flips.then: Create the provisioned deployment early to prove capacity exists.

scenarios.takeaway: Measure first, then size. Do not commit on projections.

quiz.q: Peak 600 RPM, 500-token prompts, 100-token responses, output-to-input ratio 4, cache rate 40%, 2,500 input TPM per PTU, increment 5. How many PTUs?
quiz.hint: Normalized TPM first, then divide and round up to a multiple of 5
quiz.explain: Normalized TPM = 600 x 500 x 0.6 + 4 x 600 x 100 = 180,000 + 240,000 = 420,000. Divided by 2,500 is 168, rounded up to the increment of 5 gives 170 [[r7]].

quiz.q: Which statements about PTU are correct?
options: Capacity is held whether or not requests arrive
A reservation guarantees capacity in a region
Cached tokens do not consume PTU capacity
quiz.explain: Provisioned capacity bills while idle, cached tokens are free of PTU use, and quota is not capacity. Reservations also do not guarantee capacity, so create the deployment first [[r6]].

quiz.q: A workload moves from no residency rule to an EU-only rule. Which change follows?
options: Move from Global Standard to Data Zone (EU) types
quiz.explain: Data Zone keeps processing inside the zone. Flex and quota do not change where data is processed [[r5]].

flashcards.back: No. Quota and reservations do not guarantee capacity. Create the deployment first.
Non-200 overflow from a full PTU deployment goes to a standard deployment in the same resource, for all requests or per request via `x-ms-spillover-deployment`.

flashcards.front: What is Priority processing's latency target?
flashcards.back: A p50 token rate per 5-minute window by model, for example 80 TPS for gpt-5.6-sol. It is a target, not a per-request guarantee.
